narration:
My grandmother rehearsed her own funeral the way other people rehearse job interviews. She would narrate it right there at the kitchen table, unprompted, somewhere between the coffee and the bread: who would cry too much, who would cry too little, which cousin would show up late and blame the traffic, what the priest would get wrong about her. She did this for thirty years. She outlived two of the priests.

As a child, I found it morbid. As a teenager, I found it embarrassing. And it took me until my own first rehearsals — lying awake at night, drafting the speech for a crisis that never came — to finally understand that she wasn't predicting anything. The rehearsal doesn't aim at the future. It aims at the unbearable present. And it works by borrowing the future's authority.

This is the part I keep turning over. A rehearsed catastrophe is a domesticated one. You can't control whether the flood comes, but you can control the drill — and the drill is real in a way the flood is not yet. The body performing that drill learns something true: where the exits are, what the first sentence of the terrible phone call should be. And the fact that the flood, when it comes, ignores the drill entirely — arrives by a different door, demands a different sentence — that doesn't make the drill useless. It makes it a ritual. Which is a different kind of useful.

I want to be careful here, because there are two ways to read what she was doing, and I honestly don't know which is true. She rehearsed because she couldn't stop. But that sentence refuses to choose. Was the rehearsal a compulsion — a thing that gripped her and wouldn't let go? Or was it the one thing that made stopping possible — the nightly discharge that let her put death down and finally sleep? Compulsion, or medicine. Thirty years at that kitchen table, and I cannot tell you which. And I suspect she couldn't have told you either.

What I can tell you is what the rehearsals did to us — the audience. They wore the terror smooth. By the time the real funeral came — and it came wrong, of course, on a Tuesday, in a month she had never once chosen for it — we had heard the story so many times that grief had somewhere to sit. The room was strange, but the furniture was familiar. We knew our roles, even as we failed to perform them.

I rehearse now, too. Small things: difficult conversations, the moment of being found out for crimes I haven't committed, the eulogy for people in perfect health. I don't call it morbid anymore. I call it the maintenance of furniture — keeping a place for the unbearable to sit, against the day it finally, punctually, arrives.
